title: Research
text:
Creating Quarto doc & Github Repo  Pauline Green-Williams — under review [PDF] [Code]   A project I have completed was using R analysis and Pearson correlation to determine if there was a strong correlation between hospital emergency access and fatality rates due to COVID-19. During this process I had to use web scraping from the U.S. counties and parishes list, as well as import data from the CDC website, and the bureau of labor statistics. From there I had to modify the data, join the data sets, and perform the pearson correlation test using Rstudio.
Data-generating process. Where these data came from, who produced them,and what was decided in producing them.

title: Designing my Website
text:
This website is created using Rstudio Quarto. This is my first time using Quarto but it was fairly easy to follow and understand. The theme I have shown is quartz, which I found online after searching the possible quarto site themes. I chose this theme because it is still aesthetically pleasing without being too distracting or un serious. On the home page you see a picture of me, my name, three helpful links, and a short description on what I am studying and my research interests. On the right hand side you will find a search button which allows someone to quickly jump around and find something specific on my site.
On the left hand side you will see the index which holds six tabs. My Home, Research,Teaching, CV, Github, and Email. When creating this website in its YML stage, I struggled with aligning the spacing all together, one space bar was causing the whole page to return nothing, but after reviewing the work and using AI to help highlight the problem I was able to make the necessary changes that allows the site to work. Along with creating this website we also had to create an associated github repository with it.
I’ve never used GitHub so I was originally confused on it’s purpose, but the github repository is what allows the website to actually be seen over the internet, not just the local host. The github Repository was very easy to understand and use. After creating the original template of the page adding the assignments tab was extremely easy.
I can see how having this, allows you to expand even further with the site and push the capabilities of what you want to show. My favorite part about designing this website was always updating and rendering the pages as I made changes. it was rewarding to see your hard work pay off almost immediately and kept me engaged and eager to continue on with the project.

title: Google Trends
text:
For this assignment I looked at the White house Press interest over the last 5 years.
https://trends.google.com/explore?q=white%2520house%2Cpress&date=today%205-y&geo=US&gprop=web
Whitehousepress <- gtrends(c("white house", "press", "news"),
                           onlyInterest = TRUE,
                           geo = "US",
                           gprop = "web",
                           time = "all", # last five years
                           category = 0)
the_df <- Whitehousepress$interest_over_time
plot(Whitehousepress)
write_csv(the_df, paste0("gtrends_us_5y_", Sys.Date(), ".csv"))

title: TidyCensus
text:
For this assignment I chose to look at the counties in South Carolina to examine the number of Black people living below the poverty level in the county. I chose to focus on Black as one of my variables just a personal preference because my mothers side of the family is from Charleston County. I was interested to explore the data at the tract level, but I decided to keep my analysis more general to the county level. In my Top 10 table my margins of error range between 3.88 to 7.83 percentage points. This shows that there is some sampling uncertainty surrounding the estimated Black Poverty rates. This would put be just between a commonly accepted range and less precise. In my Bottom 10 table the margins of error range between 1.90-8.77 percentage points. Some counties have a low MOE like Richland County which shows we can say this is a precise estimate and there is a limited sampling uncertainty. But when you look at Oconee County there is a 8.7% MOE which is in the less precise range, and there is some sampling uncertainty for this county. This could be from less participants in the survey for Oconee county, rather Richland county responds more.


In my case I do not have any areas in the table where the confidence intervals overlap. If I did have confidences that overlapped that would make the top 10, really a top 9 because they are technically the same rank.

title: WebScraping
text:
To run this program using my own Wikipedia source I chose a simple one which was the List of countries and dependencies by population. This was an easy enough data set that had good information but was also good for beginning web scraping.
robotstxt::paths_allowed("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population")

wiki_url <- paste0("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population")

wiki_pg <- read_html(wiki_url)
After that I pulled how many tables the data set had in the case there was more than one like the example code given. In this set there was only one table to pull from. After that I took a glimpse at the dataset that was pulled.
tabs <- wiki_pg |> html_elements("table.wikitable")
length(tabs)                      # how many candidates?
tabs |> html_table() |> lapply(\(x) dim(x))

totalpopraw <- tabs[[1]] |> html_table()
glimpse(totalpopraw)
ThenI began to clean the data set. I selected three rows to focus on which were the location, population, and date. I filtered to remove all strings that included the name world and total per the instructions. I also parsed the numbers to turn them from strings into actual numerical values in the data set. Finally we took a look at the new clean data set.
otalpop <- totalpopraw |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character),
                ~ .x |>
                  str_remove_all("\\[.*?\\]") |>   # [1], [note 2]
                  str_squish())) |>
  filter(!str_to_lower(location) %in% c("world", "location"),
         !str_to_lower(location) %in% c("total", "world total"))
totalpop <- totalpop |>
  select(location,population,date)
totalpop <- totalpop |>
  mutate(population = readr::parse_number(population))
glimpse(totalpop)
head(totalpop)
write_csv(totalpop, paste0("totalpop_wiki_", Sys.Date(), ".csv"))

title: WebScraping
text:
Data Plan
Since I do not have a designated research topic I just researched some possible data sets surrounding Education and Poverty. For our main project we are focusing on Municipal court discussion on funding surrounding the arts programs so I decided to look at data from WWW.census.gov. I am looking at the Small Area Income and Poverty Estimates for state and counties. This will be an API call rather than web scraping because the API is already given to me, which is just the more polite and safer option than web scraping. It also will be more likely that the data set is already configured in a readable way and will not require much manipulation. The robots.txt when ran in Rstudio came back as true which means that it is able to be scraped and used. When I ran the robots.txt on the back of the hyperlink I received a 404 error, but that was because it is a API link and not a webpage link. The Census Bureau allows users to query and retrieve data to analyze. There are limits to what is allowed with the data sets that are related around re-identifying personal information and combining data sets to try and identify participants. None of these limitations apply to what I will be doing with this project. The Census Bureau allows 500 request per data using the API key, but for this data set there will be a relatively low amount of queries because it is not as large as other ones. If I was using a webpage I would know that the page is broken if I tried to run the same functions or commands, and say a variable changed I would not be able to execute my code. Using an API key eliminates the worry that the data set can be randomly changed because it would have to come directly from the Census Bureau. If the link ever stops working that is how I will know that my page is changed and I need to adjust.
robotstxt::paths_allowed("https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/poverty/saipe.html")
url <- "https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/poverty/saipe"

response <- request(url) |>
  req_url_query(
    get = "NAME,SAEPOVALL_PT,SAEPOVRTALL_PT,SAEMHI_PT",
    `for` = "state:*",
    YEAR = 2024,
    key = api_key
  ) |>
  req_perform()
